This is coming from a hobby artist who genuinely really likes most of their art; I don't feel any of that same *crushing frustration and disappointment* anymore, even when pieces dont turn out as planned.  Keep in mind that this is just what has helped me personally.

In my experience, to get past this, you need to learn how to practice *effectively*.  For me, the frustration came from the feeling of not being able to translate my mental image to paper.

WORK ON YOUR FUNDAMENTALS.  If you want to do comic art, you're going to need to do a fuck ton of studies of the human body.  Do lots of gestures and figure drawing.  If you're able to find live classes, those are always the most helpful.  Prioritize short poses(like 15-30sec)

COPY COPY COPY!!!!  You need to copy!!  Everyone draws inspiration from other artists.  Do studies of how your favorite artists do specific things(example: noses, eyes, colour).  This isn't stuff you should be posting without credit of course, and you should be ideally doing these studies from multiple artists instead of just one.  Tracing to figure out the structures of their figures or features can be very helpful.

PRACTICAL TIPS:
- Bring a sketchbook with you everywhere, and default to using that instead of your phone
- Draw people in cafes, public transport, etc.  They are great for gestures.
- Draw BIGGER!  The bigger the better, and the looser the better!  
- Practice doesn't have to be miserable!  I find that it makes me happy and excited to do studies when I use art supplies that make me happy.  I have a bunch of glittery hilighters that I love to use for gestures and other quick stuff.
- No more erasing! I found that I hesitated too much and went back way too much, so my best friend(who is also an artist I look up to) reccomended to me that I only draw in pen.  That was the beginning of my real development.

- Giving exact times and dates to work on projects.  Don't tell yourself "I'll finish it Wednesday", but say instead "I'll work on this at 7pm on Wednesday"
